analogy.p: Imagine a tray of identical marbles in neat layers. If you push the top layer it rolls easily over the layer below: that is a pure metal. Now mix in some bigger and smaller marbles. The layers are jammed and cannot roll over each other so easily: that is an alloy. For the polymers, think of a bowl of spaghetti. Cooked spaghetti strands slide past each other (thermosoftening), but if the strands are glued together with cross-links the whole mass is rigid (thermosetting). The marble picture breaks down because real metal atoms are held by a sea of delocalised electrons, not just touching.

bullets: Corrosion is a **chemical reaction** between a material and its environment, not just wear or scratching.
In metals, corrosion is **oxidation**: the metal gains oxygen (or loses electrons) to form a metal oxide or other compound.
Different metals corrode at different rates: gold hardly corrodes at all, iron corrodes steadily, and aluminium is protected by a thin oxide layer.
The word **rusting** is used only for the corrosion of **iron and steel**. Aluminium, copper and zinc corrode but they do not rust.
Corrosion matters because it weakens structures, wastes resources and the energy used to extract metals, and can be dangerous (for example a corroded bridge or gas pipe).
Reducing corrosion therefore links to **sustainability**: longer-lasting metal objects mean fewer ores need to be mined and fewer metals need to be extracted.
core.p: **Corrosion** is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. For metals this means the metal reacts with oxygen, water, acids or salts in its surroundings and is slowly converted into a compound, usually an oxide, which is weaker and often useless. Corrosion costs enormous amounts of money every year because bridges, pipes, cars and ships must be repaired or replaced. It is an **oxidation** reaction because the metal atoms lose electrons and form positive ions or compounds containing oxygen.

bullets: Word equation: **iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide**.
Symbol equation (extension): 4Fe + 3O2 + 2xH2O → 2Fe2O3.xH2O, where x varies, which is why the oxide is called **hydrated** (it contains water in its structure).
Iron is **oxidised**: Fe atoms lose electrons to form Fe3+ ions in the rust.
Rust is **flaky and porous**, so it does not stop air and water reaching the iron below. Rusting therefore continues.
Salt water, acid rain and pollution (for example sulfur dioxide) speed up rusting because dissolved ions make the water a better conductor, so cars rust faster near the sea or where roads are salted.
Rust is mainly a problem for **iron and steel**, which are the most widely used metals in construction, vehicles and ships.
Rusting is **faster in warmer conditions** because particles move faster and react more often, a link to rates of reaction.
core.h: Rusting of iron: the conditions and the equation
core.p: Rusting is the corrosion of iron and its alloys (such as steel). For iron to rust, **both oxygen (from the air) and water must be present**. If either is missing, iron does not rust. The product is **hydrated iron(III) oxide**, which is the orange-brown flaky solid we call rust. Rust is porous and brittle, so it flakes off and exposes fresh iron underneath, which means rusting carries on until the whole piece may be eaten away. This is why rust is much more damaging than the thin protective oxide layer on some other metals.

bullets: Tube A: nail + anhydrous calcium chloride (dry air): **no rust**, shows water is needed.
Tube B: nail + boiled water + oil layer (no dissolved oxygen): **no rust**, shows oxygen is needed.
Tube C: nail + water + air: **rusts**, the control that shows rusting happens when both are present.
Independent variable: the conditions in the tube. **Control variables** include the type, size and mass of nail, the volume of water, the temperature and the time left.
Dependent variable: how much rust forms (observed qualitatively or by comparing mass or appearance).
The boiled water is cooled before use, otherwise the heat would speed up the reaction and spoil the fair test.
A fair test needs identical nails, so each nail is often cleaned with sandpaper first to remove any existing rust or oxide.
core.p: A classic investigation shows that both air and water are needed for rusting. Three iron nails are set up in separate test tubes. In the first, the nail is in a tube with **anhydrous calcium chloride**, a drying agent that removes water vapour from the air, so oxygen is present but water is not. In the second, the nail is in **boiled water** (boiling removes dissolved oxygen) with a layer of **oil** floating on top to stop oxygen dissolving back in, so water is present but oxygen is not. In the third, the nail is in ordinary water open to the air, so both oxygen and water are present. After several days only the third nail rusts.

bullets: **Painting** (cars, bridges, railings, ships) is cheap and also allows colour. Paint must be reapplied from time to time.
**Oil and grease** (bicycle chains, moving machine parts, tools) is used where paint would wear off because the surfaces rub together.
**Electroplating** coats the object with a thin layer of another metal (for example chromium, nickel or tin) using electricity. It gives a smart, hard-wearing finish, used on car trim and cutlery.
**Plastic coating** (for example on wire racks and dishwasher baskets) gives a thick, flexible waterproof layer.
Barrier methods only work while the layer is **unbroken**. Once scratched, air and water reach the iron and rusting begins.
With a **less reactive metal coating** such as tin on a food can, a scratch exposes the iron which then rusts faster, because iron is more reactive than tin and corrodes first.
The barrier must stop **both** oxygen and water. Saying it 'stops rust getting in' will not earn the mark.
core.p: The basic idea of a **barrier method** is to keep oxygen and water away from the iron so that the reaction cannot happen. Any coating that is waterproof and airtight will work as long as it stays intact. The coating can be applied cheaply and easily, but if it is scratched or worn away, the iron beneath is exposed and starts to rust. Different barriers suit different uses depending on how the object is used and how much protection is needed.

bullets: The sacrificial metal must be **more reactive than iron**: commonly **magnesium** or **zinc**.
Blocks of magnesium or zinc are bolted to **ship hulls**, and attached to underground pipelines and oil rigs.
The more reactive metal loses electrons: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-, so it is **oxidised** instead of the iron.
The iron stays as unreacted metal because it is not losing electrons.
The blocks gradually dissolve away, so they must be **replaced regularly**. This is a cost to include when evaluating the method.
Sacrificial protection works even if the surface is **scratched or damaged**, which is its advantage over paint.
Higher tier link: this uses the **reactivity series**. A metal can only protect iron if it is higher than iron in the series.
core.p: In **sacrificial protection** a more reactive metal is attached to the iron. Because the more reactive metal has a greater tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions, it **reacts (is oxidised) in preference to the iron**, so the iron is protected even though it is not fully covered. The more reactive metal is gradually used up, or 'sacrificed', so it must be replaced from time to time. Unlike a barrier, the protection continues even if the surface is scratched, because the sacrificial metal is still in electrical contact with the iron and still corrodes first.

bullets: Galvanising = **zinc coating** on iron or steel (usually applied by dipping the object in molten zinc).
Zinc acts as a **barrier** while the layer is complete.
If scratched, zinc still protects because it is **more reactive** and corrodes first: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-.
Compare tin plating: if tin is scratched the iron rusts **faster**, because iron is more reactive than tin.
The zinc layer slowly gets used up, so galvanised steel is not protected forever, but it lasts much longer than painted steel.
Galvanised objects can be used outdoors with little maintenance, which is a major advantage for roofs, lamp posts and guard rails.
core.h: Galvanising: barrier and sacrificial protection together
core.p: **Galvanising** is coating iron or steel with a layer of **zinc**. It protects in two ways at the same time. First, the zinc layer acts as a **barrier**, keeping air and water away from the iron. Second, zinc is more reactive than iron, so if the coating is scratched the exposed zinc around the scratch is oxidised in preference to the iron, giving **sacrificial protection**. This is why galvanised buckets, car body panels, crash barriers and steel fence posts last for many years even when they get scratched.

bullets: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, but the **oxide layer** acts as a barrier.
The oxide is **thin, hard and adheres tightly**, unlike rust which is porous and flaky.
If the layer is scratched, a new layer forms immediately in air.
This explains why aluminium is used for **aircraft, drinks cans and window frames**: low density and corrosion-resistant.
Do not say aluminium is 'unreactive'. The correct idea is that the **oxide layer protects** it.
Also note that aluminium is protected by its own oxide, whereas iron needs extra protection because its oxide is not protective.
Stainless steel works in a similar way: chromium forms a protective oxide layer.
core.p: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, yet aluminium objects such as drinks cans, window frames and aircraft last a long time. The reason is that aluminium reacts with oxygen very quickly to form a **thin, tough, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide** on its surface. This layer is **strongly attached** to the metal and is **non-porous**, so it stops air and water reaching the metal underneath and the corrosion does not continue. Unlike rust, which flakes away, aluminium oxide stays in place. This is a good example of a protective oxide layer, and the oxide layer can be thickened by a process called anodising.

bullets: Definition: alloy = a **mixture** of a metal with other elements (usually metals). It is a mixture, not a compound.
Pure metals are **soft** because layers of identical atoms slide easily.
Alloys are **harder** because atoms of different sizes disturb the regular layers.
The properties of an alloy can be **designed** by changing the proportions and the elements added.
Most **pure metals are too soft** for many uses, for example pure iron, gold and copper.
In an exam answer always mention: **different sized atoms**, **distorted layers**, and **layers cannot slide**.
Alloys are made by mixing the molten metals together and letting the mixture cool and solidify.
Alloys can still conduct electricity (metallic bonding remains) but are often a little less conductive than the pure metal.
core.h: Alloys: definition and why they are harder
core.p: An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with at least one other element, which is usually another metal (although steel contains non-metal carbon). Most metals in everyday use are alloys because pure metals are often too soft. In a pure metal the atoms are all the same size and are arranged in **regular layers**, so when a force is applied the layers can **slide over each other** easily and the metal bends or changes shape. In an alloy the atoms of the added elements are a **different size**, which **distorts the regular arrangement** of layers. This makes it **more difficult for the layers to slide**, so the alloy is **harder** and stronger than the pure metal.

bullets: **Bronze**: copper + tin. Hard, resists corrosion; used for **statues, bells, medals**.
**Brass**: copper + zinc. Harder than copper, attractive, useful for **taps, door handles, musical instruments**.
**Low carbon steel** (about 0.1% carbon): soft and easily shaped, used for **car body panels** and wire.
**High carbon steel**: harder but **brittle**, used for **tools, knives and blades**.
**Stainless steel**: iron + chromium + nickel. Hard and **resists corrosion**, used for cutlery and surgical instruments.
**Aluminium alloys**: **low density** and strong, used for **aircraft** bodies and bicycle frames.
**Gold alloys**: pure gold (24 carat) is too soft for jewellery. 18 carat gold is 18/24 = **75%** gold; 9 carat is 9/24 = **37.5%** gold.
Carats measure the proportion of gold in 24 parts, so higher carat means purer and softer.
core.p: You need to know the composition and typical uses of a set of common alloys. **Bronze** is an alloy of **copper and tin**, harder than copper and used for statues, medals and ship propellers. **Brass** is an alloy of **copper and zinc**, harder than copper and used for water taps, door fittings and musical instruments. **Steels** are alloys of **iron with carbon** (and sometimes other metals). **Aluminium alloys** are low density and used for aircraft. **Gold** for jewellery is alloyed to make it harder, and its purity is measured in carats.

bullets: **Soda-lime glass**: sand + sodium carbonate + limestone. Used for windows and bottles.
**Borosilicate glass**: sand + boron trioxide. Higher melting point; used for **lab glassware and ovenware**.
**Clay ceramics** (pottery, bricks): wet clay is **shaped** then **fired in a furnace** to harden it.
Ceramics are **hard** and have **high melting points**, but they are **brittle** and shatter on impact.
They are **poor conductors** of heat and electricity, so are used as insulators and furnace linings.
Glass is not crystalline in the way metals are: it is an **amorphous** (non-crystalline) solid, formed by cooling the melt.
Link to **bonding**: ceramics have strong ionic or covalent bonds throughout, which gives high melting points and brittleness.
core.p: **Ceramics** are non-metallic materials that are usually hard, brittle, have high melting points and are poor conductors of heat and electricity. Two types you must know are **glass** and **clay ceramics**. Most glass is **soda-lime glass**, made by heating a mixture of **sand, sodium carbonate and limestone**. **Borosilicate glass** is made from **sand and boron trioxide** and has a **higher melting point** than soda-lime glass, so it is used for laboratory glassware and ovenware that is heated strongly. **Clay ceramics** such as pottery and bricks are made by shaping wet clay and then **heating it in a furnace**, which makes it hard.

bullets: **Thermosoftening**: separate chains, **weak forces** between chains, **softens when heated**, can be remoulded. Examples: poly(ethene), PVC.
**Thermosetting**: chains joined by **strong covalent cross-links**; **do not soften** when heated; rigid. Examples: epoxy resins and Bakelite.
Cross-links are **covalent bonds between chains**, so much more energy is needed to break them than weak intermolecular forces.
Thermosoftening polymers can be **recycled** by melting; thermosetting polymers cannot.
**LDPE and HDPE**: low density and high density poly(ethene) are made by using **different catalysts and reaction conditions**.
**LDPE** has **branched chains** that cannot pack closely, so it is less dense, flexible and softens at lower temperatures (carrier bags, squeezy bottles).
**HDPE** has **straight chains** that pack closely, so it is denser, stronger and more rigid with a higher softening temperature (buckets, pipes, bottle crates).
Do not confuse the types: 'melting' of a thermosoftening polymer does not break covalent bonds, only the weak forces.
core.p: Polymers are long-chain molecules made by joining many small monomers. The way the chains are held together decides how the polymer behaves when heated. **Thermosoftening** polymers consist of **individual, tangled polymer chains** held together by **weak intermolecular forces**. When heated, these forces are easily overcome, the chains can slide past each other, and the polymer softens or melts. When cooled it hardens again, so it can be **reshaped and recycled**. **Thermosetting** polymers have **strong covalent cross-links** between chains, forming a rigid network. These cannot be melted or reshaped. On strong heating they char (burn) instead of melting.

bullets: Structure: **matrix/binder** + **reinforcement** (fibres or fragments).
**Fibreglass**: glass fibres in a plastic (polymer) matrix. Light, strong; used for boat hulls and car bodies.
**Carbon fibre**: carbon fibres in a plastic matrix; very strong and light; used for aircraft, racing cars and bikes, but expensive.
**Concrete**: aggregate (sand and gravel) in cement; **reinforced concrete** also has steel rods.
**Plywood** and **wood**: layers or fibres of wood held in a matrix of glue or lignin.
Composites are chosen because they combine properties, for example **high strength with low density**.
Disadvantages: composites can be **expensive**, are often hard to recycle, and may fail by the layers separating.
core.p: A **composite** is made of two or more different materials combined so that the final material has better properties than either alone. Most composites consist of a **matrix (or binder)** that surrounds and binds together **fibres or fragments** of another material, called the **reinforcement**. The reinforcement is often strong but brittle, and the matrix holds it in place and spreads the load. Together they give a material that is strong, light and tough. Composites can be designed for specific jobs by choosing the matrix and reinforcement.

bullets: Match each property to the **use**: aircraft need low density and strength (aluminium alloys, carbon fibre composites).
**Cooking pans**: need good thermal conductivity and corrosion resistance (copper, stainless steel).
**Cutlery**: stainless steel because it is hard and does not rust.
**Bridges and buildings**: steel for strength; reinforced concrete for compressive strength.
**Window glass**: transparent, hard and does not corrode.
**Cost** is a major factor: carbon fibre is excellent but very expensive.
**Recycling**: thermosoftening polymers and metals can be recycled; thermosets and many composites cannot easily.
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to choose the best material for a job or to compare options using data. You should match the **properties** of the material to the requirements of the use: strength, hardness, density, melting point, corrosion resistance, flexibility, electrical conductivity and cost. You should also consider the whole **life cycle**: where the raw material comes from, how much energy it takes to make, and whether it can be recycled. Use the data supplied and give reasoned comparisons, not just lists of properties.

exam: 1 mark: state the two things needed for rusting: **oxygen and water** (both required).
2 marks: explain **sacrificial protection**: a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is oxidised or loses electrons instead of the iron.
2 marks: **barrier** methods: the coating stops oxygen and water reaching the iron; add that it fails if scratched.
3 marks: why alloys are harder: **different sized atoms** distort the layers, so the layers **cannot slide** easily.
Compare **galvanising and painting**: both barriers, but zinc also protects sacrificially when scratched.
Command word **explain** needs a reason (because...). **Describe** needs facts only. **Evaluate** needs advantages, disadvantages and a judgement.
For **polymers** use 'weak intermolecular forces between chains' versus 'strong covalent cross-links'.
For **composites** name both parts: matrix (binder) and reinforcement (fibres or fragments), and give an example such as fibreglass.
Gold carat questions: **mass of gold = (carats ÷ 24) × mass of ring**. Show the working for the method marks.
6 mark questions: structure the answer, for example for each material state a property, link it to the use, then give a comparison and a conclusion.
Use the correct names: **hydrated iron(III) oxide**, **thermosoftening**, **thermosetting**, **matrix**, **reinforcement**.

mistakes.r: Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Give both in every answer.
mistakes.w: Iron rusts because it reacts with oxygen.

mistakes.r: Rust is flaky and porous so it does not protect; the oxide layer on aluminium is thin, tight and non-porous.
mistakes.w: Rust forms a protective layer like aluminium oxide.

mistakes.r: Aluminium is reactive but protected by a thin layer of aluminium oxide.
mistakes.w: Aluminium does not corrode because it is unreactive.

mistakes.r: Paint is a barrier. Sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal that is oxidised instead of iron.
mistakes.w: Paint or sacrificial protection are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Galvanising works as a barrier and by sacrificial protection if scratched, because zinc is more reactive than iron.
mistakes.w: Zinc protects iron by covering it only.

mistakes.r: Different sized atoms distort the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other easily.
mistakes.w: Alloys are harder because the atoms are bonded together more strongly.

mistakes.r: An alloy is a mixture of metals (and sometimes other elements) so the elements are not chemically combined.
Only the weak forces between chains are overcome. The covalent bonds in the chains stay intact.
mistakes.w: Thermosoftening polymers melt because covalent bonds break.

mistakes.r: Thermosetting polymers have strong covalent cross-links between chains, so they do not melt.
mistakes.w: Thermosetting polymers have weaker bonds than thermosoftening ones.

summary: You must explain corrosion and rusting and how it is prevented by barriers, sacrificial protection and galvanising, and why alloys are harder than pure metals. You also need the composition and uses of common alloys, ceramics, thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers (including LDPE and HDPE) and composites. It matters because choosing the right material for a job is a common exam application.

terms.d: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.
The corrosion of iron or steel in the presence of oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide.
Hydrated iron(III) oxide, a flaky orange-brown solid.
A coating such as paint, oil, grease or a plated metal that keeps oxygen and water away from the metal.
Coating an object with a thin layer of metal using electricity.
Attaching a more reactive metal to iron so that the more reactive metal is oxidised in preference to the iron.
Coating iron or steel with zinc, which acts as a barrier and as a sacrificial metal.
A mixture of a metal with at least one other element, usually another metal.
A measure of the purity of gold: 24 carat is pure gold; 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron with carbon and sometimes other metals.
A non-metallic material that is hard, brittle and has a high melting point, such as glass, pottery and bricks.
A polymer with weak forces between individual chains, which softens when heated and can be reshaped.
A polymer with strong covalent cross-links between chains that does not soften when heated.
A covalent bond joining one polymer chain to another.
A material made of a matrix (binder) surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a reinforcement.
The material in a composite that surrounds and binds the reinforcement.
The fibres or fragments in a composite that are held in place by the matrix.
Low density and high density poly(ethene), made with different catalysts and conditions.

worked.q: An 18 carat gold ring has a mass of 6.0 g. (a) What percentage of the ring is gold? (b) Calculate the mass of gold in the ring. (3 marks)
steps: Pure gold is 24 carat, so 18 carat means 18 parts gold in 24.
Mass of gold = 75% of 6.0 g = 0.75 × 6.0 = 4.5 g.

worked.ans: Zinc is a barrier and, because it is more reactive than iron, it is oxidised instead of the iron if scratched (sacrificial protection), so galvanised steel stays protected even when damaged, whereas paint fails once scratched.
worked.q: Explain why the steel body of a car is galvanised instead of just painted. (4 marks)
steps: Galvanising puts a layer of zinc on the steel, which is a barrier keeping out oxygen and water.
Paint is also a barrier but if it is scratched the iron is exposed and rusts.
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so if the zinc layer is scratched, the zinc loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference to the iron.
So the iron is still protected, which is called sacrificial protection.

worked.ans: Brass contains atoms of different sizes which distort the regular arrangement of layers, making it harder for layers to slide, so brass is harder than pure copper.
worked.q: Explain why an alloy such as brass is harder than pure copper. (3 marks)
steps: In pure copper the atoms are all the same size and arranged in regular layers.
The layers can slide over each other easily, so copper is soft.
In brass, zinc atoms are a different size, which distorts the layers, so the layers cannot slide as easily.
